'''William Graham Richards''' (1 October 1939 – 11 February 2025) was an English chemist and [[Fellow]] of [[Brasenose College, Oxford]].<ref name="Hundred">{{cite web |title=Professor Graham Richards in top 100 British Scientists list |url=https://www.bnc.ox.ac.uk/about-brasenose/news/857-professor-graham-richards-in-top-100-british-scientists-list |access-date=24 May 2018 |website=Brasenose College}}</ref> He served as head of the department of chemistry at the [[University of Oxford]] from 1997 to 2006.<ref name="Howard"/>

Richards was a pioneer in the field of computer-aided molecular design, in particular its application to the pharmaceuticals industry. He was the founding scientist of Oxford Molecular Ltd.,<ref name="FRS"/> and introduced a novel model for the funding of research at Oxford University, which has been copied elsewhere.<ref name="Owen"/><ref>{{cite web|title=Make money without losing your soul|url=https://www.harriman-house.com/press/full/593|website=Harriman House|access-date=25 May 2018}}</ref> Richards was one of the scientific co-founders of Oxford Molecular Limited (OMG). The company developed software for modelling of small molecules and proteins, and drug design. Benefiting from the economic and legal changes, the company was floated on the London Stock Exchange in 1992, making the university £10 million. The company was worth £450 million at its peak but was eventually sold for £70 million. Richards published more than 300 scientific papers,<ref name="Biospace">{{cite news|title=Graham Richards Joins Science Advisory Panel at Oxford Medical Diagnostics|url=https://www.biospace.com/b-graham-richards-b-joins-science-advisory-panel-at-b-oxford-medical-diagnostics-b|access-date=25 May 2018|work=Biospace|date=24 January 2011}}</ref> including 15 books.

==Education==
Graham Richards was born on 1 October 1939 in [[Hoylake]], England, to Percy Richards and Gwendoline Julia Richards (née Evans).<ref>Entry in Register of Births for Wirral 4th qtr of 1939 vol 8a page 1143 William G born to Richards and Evans</ref><ref name="Nordling"/> Both parents were of [[Welsh people|Welsh]] extraction.<ref name="Nordling"/> Richards was educated at [[Birkenhead School]].<ref name="Periodic"/> He won a scholarship to [[Brasenose College, Oxford]], starting his studies there in 1958.<ref name="Periodic">{{cite journal
|journal=Periodic the Magazine of the Department of Chemistry
|date=October 2017
|title=The Lucky Chemist
|first=Graham
|last=Richards
}}</ref> 

He received his bachelor's degree in Chemistry with first class honours from the University of Oxford<ref name="Howard">{{cite journal|last1=Howard|first1=Brian J.|last2=Grant|first2=Guy H.|title=(William) Graham Richards|journal=Molecular Physics|date= 2009|volume=101|issue=17|pages=2647–2657|doi=10.1080/00268970310001605741
|s2cid=95031061}}</ref> in 1961.<ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.chem.ox.ac.uk/article/professor-graham-richards-cbe-frs |title=Professor Graham Richards CBE FRS |publisher=Department of Chemistry, University of Oxford |access-date=2026-05-05}}</ref> He then studied the [[electronic spectroscopy]] of [[diatomic molecules]] with Richard F. Barrow,<ref name="Howard"/> earning his Master of Arts and [[Doctor of Philosophy]]<ref name=grdphil>{{cite thesis|degree=DPhil|publisher=University of Oxford|url=https://copac.jisc.ac.uk/id/41488337?style=html|title=Electronic spectra of simple molecules|first=William Graham|last=Richards|date=1964|id={{EThOS|uk.bl.ethos.710535}}|access-date=5 February 2019|archive-date=7 February 2019|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190207072311/https://copac.jisc.ac.uk/id/41488337?style=html|url-status=dead}}</ref> degrees from the University of Oxford in 1964.<ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.chem.ox.ac.uk/article/professor-graham-richards-cbe-frs |title=Professor Graham Richards CBE FRS |publisher=Department of Chemistry, University of Oxford |access-date=2026-05-05}}</ref>

==Career and research==
After his DPhil, Richards continued his spectroscopic work with fellowships in Oxford (ICI Research Fellowship, Junior Research Fellowship at Balliol College) and Paris, France (Centre de Mécanique Ondulatoire Appliquée).<ref name="CT">{{cite web|title=W. Graham Richards|url=https://academictree.org/chemistry/peopleinfo.php?pid=66025|website=Chemistry Tree|access-date=23 May 2018}}</ref>

He soon returned to Oxford as a research fellow at [[Balliol College, Oxford]] (1964–1966), before being elected to a Fellowship in Chemistry at [[Brasenose College, Oxford|Brasenose College]] (1966–2007), his alma mater.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Diamantis |first=Julia |title=Professor Graham Richards - Brasenose College, Oxford |url=https://www.bnc.ox.ac.uk/about-brasenose/news/2909-professor-graham-richards |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20250701115730/https://www.bnc.ox.ac.uk/about-brasenose/news/2909-professor-graham-richards |archive-date=2025-07-01 |access-date=2025-08-21 |website=www.bnc.ox.ac.uk |language=en-gb}}</ref> He was promoted to a lecturer at Oxford University (1966–1994), to reader (1994–1996), and to professor (1996–2007). He served as chairman of the chemistry department from 1997 to 2006.<ref name="Howard"/> Richards celebrated his formal retirement from the University of Oxford on 18 May 2007.<ref name="Brazen">{{cite journal|title=An address given by Graham Richards on the occasion of his retirement dinner 19 May 2007|url=https://www.bnc.ox.ac.uk/downloads/brazen_notes/brazen_nose_2007.pdf|journal=The Brazen Nose|volume=41|pages=127–129|date=2007|access-date=23 May 2018|archive-date=13 August 2021|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210813191107/https://www.bnc.ox.ac.uk/downloads/brazen_notes/brazen_nose_2007.pdf|url-status=dead}}</ref>

===Industry involvement===
In the fourth year of his degree course Richards' research project led him to using Oxford's [[Ferranti Mercury]] computer to solve [[integrals]].<ref name="Nordling"/>
During a fellowship year in France at Centre de Mécanique Ondulatoire Appliquée, he was able to use more powerful computers.<ref name="Fifty">{{cite book|last1=Richards|first1=Graham|title=50 years at Oxford|date=2011|publisher=AuthorHouse|location=Bloomington, IN|isbn=978-1-4567-7861-3|pages=19–20|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=q4GwJFtof68C&pg=PA19|access-date=24 May 2018}}</ref> 
Returning to Oxford, he worked on [[Ab initio quantum chemistry methods|''ab initio'' computations]] and applied computational techniques to solving [[quantum mechanics|quantum mechanical]] problems in theoretical chemistry, in particular studying [[spin-orbit coupling]].<ref name="FRS"/>

His influential paper ''Third age of quantum chemistry'' (1979) marked the development of computational techniques for theoretical analysis whose precision equaled or surpassed experimental results.<ref name="McDouall">{{cite book|last1=McDouall|first1=Joseph J.W.|title=Computational quantum chemistry : molecular structure and properties in silico|date=2013|publisher=Royal Society of Chemistry|location=Cambridge|isbn=978-1-84973-608-4|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=AmwoDwAAQBAJ&pg=PT15}}</ref><ref name="Yarkony">{{cite book|last1=Yarkony|first1=David R.|title=Modern electronic structure theory.|date=1995|publisher=World Scientific|location=Singapore|isbn=978-981-283-211-5|page=4|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=p7vACwAAQBAJ&pg=PA4|access-date=25 May 2018}}</ref><ref name="Nature1979">{{cite journal|last1=Richards|first1=Graham|title=Third age of quantum chemistry|journal=Nature|date=5 April 1979|volume=278|issue=5704|pages=507–8|doi=10.1038/278507a0|pmid=431715|bibcode=1979Natur.278..507R|s2cid=38282128|doi-access=free}}</ref>

{{blockquote|"The work represents perhaps a near perfect instance of theory being in harmony with experiment, each aspect vital to the other and the combination much more than the sum of the separate parts." – Graham Richards<ref name="Nature1979"/><ref name="McDouall"/>}}

Richards saw the potential to apply computer techniques for examining the structure and properties of compounds in the area of pharmaceutical applications. He became a pioneer in the field of computer-aided molecular design. He was the first to produce coloured images modelling molecular structure graphically,<ref name="Nordling"/> and introduced many of the techniques now widely used in academia and industry.<ref name="FRS"/>

In 1982, Richards became a founding member of the [[Molecular Graphics]] Society (now the Molecular Graphics and Modelling Society, MGMS).<ref name="MGMS">{{cite web|title=Honorary Members of the MGMS Community|url=https://www.mgms.org/membership.html|website=Molecular Graphics and Modelling Society|access-date=23 May 2018}}</ref> The society started the ''Journal of Molecular Graphics'' in 1983. He served as the editor-in-chief of the journal from 1984 to 1996. The journal's name changed to ''Journal of Molecular Graphics and Modelling'' in 1997.<ref name="Willett">{{cite journal|last1=Willett|first1=P.|title=A bibliometric analysis of the Journal of Molecular Graphics and Modelling|journal=Journal of Molecular Graphics and Modelling|date=2007|volume=26|issue=3|pages=602–606|url=https://eprints.whiterose.ac.uk/3544/1/willettp-1.pdf|access-date=25 May 2018|doi=10.1016/j.jmgm.2007.03.008|pmid=17434326|bibcode=2007JMGM...26..602W |s2cid=20443291 }}</ref>

In 1989, Richards was the scientific co-founder (with [[Tony Marchington]], David Ricketts, [[James Hiddleston]], and [[Anthony Rees]]) of Oxford Molecular Limited. The company developed software for modelling of small molecules and proteins, and drug design.<ref name="Sadek">{{cite book|last1=Sadek|first1=Hassan A.|title=Bioinformatics : principles, basic internet applications|page=28|date=2004 |isbn=978-1-4120-2517-1|publisher=Trafford|location=Victoria, B.C. |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=NPByF1XHsQMC&pg=PA28|access-date=23 May 2018}}</ref> 

The company was possible in part because of economic and legal changes under the government of [[Margaret Thatcher]] that enabled British universities to become involved with [[venture capital]] and [[technology transfer]]. As Oxford Molecular Group, Ltd. (OMG) the company was floated on the London Stock Exchange in 1992, making the university £10 million. The company was worth £450 million at its peak but was eventually sold for £70 million.<ref name="Nordling"/><ref name="IP Group"/> It was one of several companies that combined to form [[Accelrys]] in 2001.<ref name="Accelrys">{{cite web|author=Accelrys |title=Pharmacopeia Inc. Announces Accelrys, a New Leader in Scientific Software – Accelrys to Represent the Best in Software for Chemical and Pharmaceutial Research|url=http://www.evaluategroup.com/Universal/View.aspx?type=Story&id=8567|access-date=25 May 2018|website=Evaluate|date=2 April 2001}}</ref>

Richards was instrumental in raising £64 million to fund a new laboratory for Oxford University through an innovative funding approach. £20 million worth of funding began with an "unusual collaboration" between Richards and [[David Norwood]].<ref name="Owen"/> Norwood then arranged for Beeson-Gregory to provide £20 million in exchange for half the University's equity share of any spin-out companies emanating from the Chemistry Department for 15 years. In 2003, Beeson-Gregory and [[Evolution Group]] merged, later creating a subsidiary, IP2IPO ("Intellectual property to initial public offering").<ref name="Owen">{{cite book|last1=Owen|first1=Geoffrey|last2=Hopkins|first2=Michael M.|title=Science, the State and the City: Britain's Struggle to Succeed in Biotechnology|date=2016|publisher=Oxford University Press|isbn=978-0-19-872800-9|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=cBz4CwAAQBAJ&pg=PA83|access-date=23 May 2018}}</ref><ref name="Lawton-Smith">{{cite book|last1=Lawton-Smith|first1=Helen|title=Universities and the economy|date=2005|publisher=Routledge, an imprint of Taylor & Francis Books Ltd|location=London|isbn=978-0-415-32493-9|page=188|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=HR6AAgAAQBAJ&pg=PA188|access-date=23 May 2018}}</ref> 
Richards became a non-executive director of IP2IPO in 2001, and non-executive chairman of IP2IPO in 2004.<ref name="IP Group">{{cite web|title=Graham Richards to become Non-Executive Chairman of the Company|url=https://www.ipgroupplc.com/media/ip-group-news/pre-2007/2004-08-10|website=IP Group|access-date=23 May 2018}}</ref>

Through this arrangement the Chemistry Department has contributed over £100 million to the University of Oxford.<ref name="Periodic"/>

Richards served as a director of ISIS Innovation Ltd., the University of Oxford's technology transfer company.<ref name="Biospace"/> It became [[Oxford University Innovation]] as of June 2016.<ref name="II">{{cite web|title=Isis Innovation becomes Oxford University Innovation|url=http://www.ox.ac.uk/staff/news-listing/2016-06-23-isis-innovation-becomes-oxford-university-innovation|website=University of Oxford|access-date=25 May 2018|date=23 June 2016}}</ref>
It has brought around 60 spin-out companies into existence.<ref name="Nordling">{{cite news|last1=Nordling|first1=Linda|title=Spin-out doctor|url=https://www.theguardian.com/education/2009/feb/10/graham-richards|access-date=23 May 2018|work=The Guardian|date=9 February 2009}}</ref>

The ''Financial Times'' has described the approach as "the way universities should be financed in the future".<ref name="Lawton-Smith"/>{{rp|188}}

Richards also introduced the use of [[distributed computing]] in pharmaceutical design. Started in 2000, his Screensaver Lifesaver project exploited idle time on more than 3.5 million personal computers in over 200 countries, whose owners agreed to be involved and downloaded the project's [[screensaver]]. Using idle time from these computers, the project's software created a virtual supercomputer that screened billions of compounds against protein targets, searching for possible drug treatments for [[cancer]], [[anthrax]] and [[smallpox]].<ref name="FRS"/><ref name="Stoller"/><ref name="Collins">{{cite journal|last1=Collins|first1=Luke |title=Hooked to computers|journal=IEE Review |date=2003 |volume=49|issue=10|url=https://ieeexplore.ieee.org/document/1250444|access-date=25 May 2018}}</ref>
The project involved collaboration between [[Intel]], [[United Devices]], and the Centre for Computational Drug Discovery at the University of Oxford,<ref name="Freemantle"/> headed by Richards<ref name="Biospace"/> and funded by the [[National Foundation for Cancer Research]] (NFCR).<ref name="Freemantle">{{cite news|last1=Freemantle |first1=Michael|work=Chemical and Engineering News |title=PC users can help cancer research |url=http://pubs.acs.org/cen/topstory/7915/7915notw3.html|access-date=25 May 2018 |volume=79|issue=15|page=6|date=9 April 2001}}</ref>

Richards formed the spin-out company InhibOx Ltd. in 2001.<ref name="Sansom">{{cite web|last1=Sansom|first1=Clare |title=Countdown to the last antibiotic|date= March 2018 |url=https://www.chemistryworld.com/feature/the-antibiotic-countdown/3008544.article|website=Chemistry World|access-date=25 May 2018}}</ref><ref name="Periodic"/> InhibOx applied [[cloud computing]] techniques to [[computational chemistry]] and drug discovery, and developed a searchable database of small-molecules called Scopius.<ref name="REF2014">{{cite web|title=UOA08-09: Computational chemistry to facilitate drug development|url=https://impact.ref.ac.uk/CaseStudies/CaseStudy.aspx?Id=18224|website=REF2014|access-date=25 May 2018}}</ref> In 2002, Richards donated his shares, twenty-five per cent of the company, to the National Foundation for Cancer Research.<ref name="Simpkins">{{cite news|last1=Simpkins|first1=Edward|title=Cancer professor gives shares to charity|url=https://www.telegraph.co.uk/finance/2746669/Cancer-professor-gives-shares-to-charity.html|access-date=23 May 2018|work=The Telegraph|date=23 December 2001}}</ref><ref name="Stoller">{{cite web|last1=Stoller|first1=Robyn|title=NFCR-Funded Project in Early 2000s Leads to Progress Today in Computational Drug Design|url=https://www.nfcr.org/blog/blognfcr-funded-project-early-2000s-leads-progress-today-computational-drug-design/|access-date=24 May 2018|website=National Foundation for Cancer Research|date=21 March 2017}}</ref> In 2017, InhibOx relaunched as Oxford Drug Design Ltd.,<ref name="OT">{{cite web|title=Head-to-head with Paul Finn at Oxford Drug Design|url=http://theoxfordtrust.co.uk/2018/02/12/head-head-paul-finn-oxford-drug-design/|website=The Oxford Trust|access-date=25 May 2018|date=12 February 2018|archive-date=26 May 2018|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180526112706/http://theoxfordtrust.co.uk/2018/02/12/head-head-paul-finn-oxford-drug-design/|url-status=dead}}</ref> with a new focus on antibiotic discovery.<ref name="Sansom"/>

{{As of |2011}} Richards joined the Science Advisory Panel of Oxford Medical Diagnostics.<ref name="Biospace"/>
He was a non-executive director of IP Group plc, having also served as its chairman.<ref name="FRS"/><ref name="Mawson">{{cite web|last1=Mawson|first1=James|title=Investment Unit of the Year: IP Group The UK-based investor wins this year's investment award|website=Global University Venturing|date=22 October 2014|url=http://www.globaluniversityventuring.com/article.php/4045/investment-unit-of-the-year-ip-group|access-date=25 May 2018|archive-date=26 May 2018|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180526042038/http://www.globaluniversityventuring.com/article.php/4045/investment-unit-of-the-year-ip-group|url-status=dead}}</ref>

==Personal life and death==
Richards married his first wife, Jessamy Kershaw, on 12 December 1970. She died of cancer in November 1988. On 5 October 1996, Richards married Mary Elizabeth Phillips, director of research planning at [[University College London]]. He had two sons and three stepchildren.<ref name="Nordling"/> Richards died on 11 February 2025, at the age of 85.<ref name="BNCNews">{{cite news|title=Professor Graham Richards|url=https://www.bnc.ox.ac.uk/about-brasenose/news/2909-professor-graham-richards/|access-date=25 May 2018|work=Brasenose College|date=12 February 2025}}</ref>

===Awards and honours===
Richards was a council member of the [[Royal Society of Chemistry]] and of the [[Royal Institution]], and a [[Fellow of the Royal Society]],<ref name="FRS"/> and was appointed [[Commander of the Order of the British Empire]] (CBE) in the [[2001 Birthday Honours]] for services to Chemistry.<ref>United Kingdom {{London Gazette| issue=56237 |date=16 June 2001|pages=9 |supp=1}}</ref> The ''[[Times Higher Education Supplement]]'' (2006) considered Richards to be one of twelve academic "super-earners" in the United Kingdom.<ref name="Nordling"/><ref name="Shepherd">{{cite news|last1=Shepherd|first1=J.|title=Academics strike gold|url=https://www.timeshighereducation.com/news/academics-strike-gold/200836.article|access-date=24 May 2018|work=Times Higher Education Supplement|date=20 January 2006|page=1}}</ref>
''Times'' magazine's first ''Eureka'' issue (2010) included Richards in its list of the top 100 British scientists.<ref name="Eureka">{{cite news|title=Eureka 100: the people that matter The 100 most important people in British science|url=https://www.thetimes.com/uk/science/article/eureka-100-the-people-that-matter-bxd3ss79tb5|access-date=24 May 2018|work=[[The Times]]|issue=Eureka|date=7 October 2010}}</ref> Richards' work has been acknowledged through a number of more formal awards and honours, including:
* 2018, [[Fellow of the Royal Society]] (FRS)<ref name="FRS">{{cite web|title=Graham Richards|url=https://royalsociety.org/people/graham-richards-13838/|website=The Royal Society|access-date=23 May 2018}}</ref>
* 2018, [[Richard J. Bolte Sr. Award]] by the [[Science History Institute]]<ref name="Bolte">{{cite web|title= Richard J. Bolte Sr. Award for Supporting Industries |url=https://www.sciencehistory.org/richard-j-bolte-sr-award-for-supporting-industries|website=Science History Institute|access-date=1 February 2018|date=31 May 2016}}</ref>
* 2017, [[Fellow of the Royal Society of Chemistry|Honorary Fellow of the Royal Society of Chemistry]] (HonFRSC)<ref>{{cite web|title=Honorary Fellows at the Royal Society of Chemistry|url=https://www.rsc.org/about-us/our-history/our-honorary-fellows/#undefined|access-date=14 February 2025|website=[[Royal Society of Chemistry]] |date=8 June 2016 }}</ref>
* 2011, Fellow of the [[Learned Society of Wales]]<ref name="Hundred"/><ref>{{cite web|title=Fellows|url=https://www.learnedsociety.wales/our-fellows/fellows/|website=The Learned Society of Wales|access-date=25 May 2018}}</ref>
* 2010, Co-Vice-President of the [[Royal Society of Chemistry]]<ref name="Hundred"/>
* 2004, Award of the [[American Chemical Society]] for Computers in Chemical and Pharmaceutical Research<ref name="ACS2004">{{cite journal|title=AWARDS|journal=Chemical & Engineering News|date=September 2003|volume=81|issue=35|pages=33–34|doi=10.1021/cen-v081n035.p033|doi-access=free}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|title=ACS Award for Computers in Chemical and Pharmaceutical Research|url=https://www.acs.org/content/acs/en/funding-and-awards/awards/national/bytopic/acs-award-for-computers-in-chemical-and-pharmaceutical-research.html|website=American Chemical Society|access-date=25 May 2018}}</ref><ref name="Diatomics">{{cite journal|last1=Richards|first1=W. Graham|title=From Diatomics to Drugs and Distributions|journal=Journal of Medicinal Chemistry|date=January 2005|volume=48|issue=2|pages=337–344|doi=10.1021/jm040136y|pmid=15658845}}</ref>
* 2001, [[Order of the British Empire|Commander of the Order of the British Empire]], Queen's Birthday Honours<ref>{{cite web|title=REPORT OF DR. LEE'S PROFESSOR OF CHEMISTRY FOR THE YEAR ENDED 31st JULY 2001|url=http://ptclweb.chem.ox.ac.uk/Data/Sites/52/media/annrep01.pdf|website=University of Oxford|access-date=25 May 2018|archive-date=26 February 2018|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180226094400/http://ptclweb.chem.ox.ac.uk/Data/Sites/52/media/annrep01.pdf|url-status=dead}}</ref>
* 1996, The Lord Lloyd of Kilgerran Award, [[Foundation for Science and Technology]]<ref name="Kilgerran">{{cite journal|title=The Lord Lloyd of Kilgerran Award: Previous winners of the award|journal=The Journal of the Foundation for Science and Technology |date=July 2007|volume=19|issue=5|page=23|url=https://www.foundation.org.uk/journal/pdf/fst_19_05.pdf|access-date=25 May 2018}}</ref>
* 1998, [[Mullard Award]], [[Royal Society]]<ref name="FRS"/>
* 1972, Marlow Medal, [[Royal Society of Chemistry]]<ref>{{cite web|title=Marlow Award Previous Winners|url=http://www.rsc.org/ScienceAndTechnology/Awards/MarlowAward/PreviousWinners.asp|website=[[Royal Society of Chemistry]]|access-date=25 May 2018}}</ref>
